## SECTION C: MEDIUM ANSWER QUESTIONS (2 marks each) - 100 Questions

**Instructions:** Write answers in 3-4 sentences or provide labeled diagrams where asked.

1. Explain the classification of meristematic tissues based on position.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Meristematic tissues are classified based on their position in the plant body into three types: apical meristems, found at the tips of roots and shoots; intercalary meristems, found between mature tissues; and lateral meristems, found in the mature regions of roots and shoots.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

2. Describe the characteristics and functions of parenchyma tissue.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Parenchyma tissue is composed of thin-walled, isodiametric cells with intercellular spaces. It performs various functions such as photosynthesis, storage, and secretion.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

3. Compare parenchyma and collenchyma tissues.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Parenchyma cells have thin walls and are involved in storage and photosynthesis, while collenchyma cells have thickened corners and provide mechanical support to growing parts of the plant.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

4. Explain the structure and function of sclerenchyma tissue.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Sclerenchyma tissue is composed of long, narrow cells with thick, lignified walls. It provides mechanical support to the organs and can be of two types: fibres and sclereids.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

5. Describe the composition and function of xylem tissue.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Xylem is a complex tissue that conducts water and minerals from the roots to the rest of the plant. It is composed of four elements: tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres, and xylem parenchyma.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

6. Explain the composition and function of phloem tissue.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Phloem is a complex tissue that transports food materials from the leaves to other parts of the plant. It is composed of four elements: sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, and phloem fibres.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

7. Differentiate between simple and complex tissues.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Simple tissues are made up of only one type of cell, while complex tissues are made up of more than one type of cell. Parenchyma is a simple tissue, while xylem is a complex tissue.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

8. Describe the epidermal tissue system.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The epidermal tissue system forms the outermost covering of the plant body. It consists of epidermal cells, stomata, and epidermal appendages like trichomes and hairs.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

9. Explain the ground tissue system.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The ground tissue system includes all tissues except the epidermis and vascular bundles. It is composed of simple tissues like parenchyma, collenchyma, and sclerenchyma.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

10. Describe the vascular tissue system.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The vascular tissue system consists of the complex tissues, xylem and phloem, which are responsible for the transport of water, minerals, and food.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

11. Compare the anatomy of dicot and monocot roots.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Dicot roots have a tap root system, while monocot roots have a fibrous root system. Dicot roots have fewer xylem bundles (2-4), while monocot roots have more (polyarch). The pith is small in dicot roots and large in monocot roots.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

12. Explain the structure of dicot root with emphasis on stele.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The stele of a dicot root consists of the pericycle, vascular bundles, and pith. The vascular bundles are arranged in a radial manner, with xylem and phloem on different radii. The xylem is exarch, with the protoxylem towards the periphery.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

13. Describe the endodermis and its significance.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The endodermis is the innermost layer of the cortex in a root. It contains Casparian strips, which are impermeable to water and regulate the movement of water and minerals into the vascular cylinder.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

14. Explain the concept of exarch and endarch conditions.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Exarch condition is when the protoxylem is towards the periphery, as seen in roots. Endarch condition is when the protoxylem is towards the center, as seen in stems.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

15. Compare the pith in dicot and monocot roots.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The pith in a dicot root is small or inconspicuous, while the pith in a monocot root is large and well-developed.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

16. Describe the anatomy of dicot stem.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

A dicot stem has an epidermis, a cortex divided into hypodermis, cortical layers, and endodermis, and a stele with vascular bundles arranged in a ring.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

17. Explain the arrangement of vascular bundles in dicot stem.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The vascular bundles in a dicot stem are arranged in a ring. They are conjoint, collateral, and open, meaning they have a cambium between the xylem and phloem.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

18. Describe the anatomy of monocot stem.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

A monocot stem has a sclerenchymatous hypodermis, scattered vascular bundles, and a large parenchymatous ground tissue. The vascular bundles are conjoint, collateral, and closed.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

19. Compare the vascular bundles of dicot and monocot stems.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Dicot stem vascular bundles are arranged in a ring and are open, while monocot stem vascular bundles are scattered and are closed.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

20. Explain the structure of dicot leaf.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

A dicot leaf is dorsiventral, with a distinct upper and lower surface. The mesophyll is differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

21. Describe the mesophyll organization in dicot leaf.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The mesophyll in a dicot leaf is differentiated into an upper palisade parenchyma with elongated cells and a lower spongy parenchyma with loosely arranged cells and large air cavities.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

22. Explain the structure of monocot leaf.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

A monocot leaf is isobilateral, with similar upper and lower surfaces. The mesophyll is not differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

23. Compare dicot and monocot leaves.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Dicot leaves are dorsiventral with more stomata on the lower surface, while monocot leaves are isobilateral with stomata on both surfaces. The mesophyll is differentiated in dicot leaves but not in monocot leaves.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

24. Describe the function and structure of bulliform cells.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Bulliform cells are large, empty, colorless cells found in the epidermis of grasses. They help in the rolling and unrolling of leaves in response to water availability, thus reducing water loss.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

25. Explain the significance of stomata in plant anatomy.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Stomata are pores in the epidermis of leaves that regulate the exchange of gases (carbon dioxide and oxygen) and water vapor between the plant and the atmosphere.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

26. Describe the types of vascular bundles based on arrangement.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Vascular bundles can be arranged in a radial manner (in roots) or a conjoint manner (in stems). Conjoint bundles can be collateral (phloem on one side of xylem) or bicollateral (phloem on both sides of xylem).

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

27. Explain open and closed vascular bundles.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Open vascular bundles have a cambium between the xylem and phloem, allowing for secondary growth. Closed vascular bundles lack a cambium and do not undergo secondary growth.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

28. Describe the secondary growth in dicot stem.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Secondary growth in a dicot stem occurs due to the activity of the vascular cambium, which produces secondary xylem and phloem, leading to an increase in the girth of the stem.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

29. Explain the formation of annual rings.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Annual rings are formed due to the differential activity of the cambium in different seasons. In spring, the cambium is more active and produces larger vessels (springwood), while in autumn, it is less active and produces smaller vessels (autumnwood). The two types of wood together form an annual ring.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

30. Describe the structure and function of cambium.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The cambium is a layer of meristematic tissue that is responsible for secondary growth. It is located between the xylem and phloem and produces secondary xylem to the inside and secondary phloem to the outside.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

31. Explain the difference between heartwood and sapwood.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Heartwood is the central, non-functional, and dark-colored wood of a tree, while sapwood is the outer, functional, and light-colored wood that conducts water.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

32. Describe the formation of bark.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Bark is formed by the activity of the cork cambium, which produces cork to the outside and phelloderm to the inside. Bark includes all the tissues outside the vascular cambium.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

33. Explain the structure and function of lenticels.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Lenticels are pores in the periderm of woody stems that allow for the exchange of gases between the internal tissues and the atmosphere.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

34. Describe the periderm formation.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Periderm is formed during secondary growth and consists of the cork cambium, the cork (phellem) it produces on the outside, and the phelloderm (secondary cortex) it produces on the inside.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

35. Explain the types of secretory structures in plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Secretory structures in plants can be laticiferous ducts (producing latex), resin ducts, nectaries, or hydathodes.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

36. Describe the structure and function of laticiferous ducts.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Laticiferous ducts are specialized tubes that are present in some plants and produce a milky fluid called latex.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

37. Explain the different types of crystals found in plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Plants can have various types of crystals, such as raphides (needle-shaped), druses (spherical clusters), and cystoliths (deposits of calcium carbonate).

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

38. Describe the storage of secondary metabolites in plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Secondary metabolites, such as alkaloids, tannins, and essential oils, are stored in various parts of the plant, often in specialized cells or vacuoles.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

39. Explain the adaptation of xerophytic plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Xerophytic plants have adaptations to conserve water, such as a thick cuticle, sunken stomata, and succulent leaves or stems.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

40. Describe the anatomy of hydrophytic plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Hydrophytic plants have adaptations to live in water, such as aerenchyma for buoyancy, reduced vascular tissue, and finely dissected leaves.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

41. Explain the concept of aerenchyma in aquatic plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Aerenchyma is a type of parenchyma with large air spaces that provides buoyancy to aquatic plants and allows for the diffusion of gases.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

42. Describe the mechanical tissues and their distribution.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Mechanical tissues, such as collenchyma and sclerenchyma, provide support to the plant body. Collenchyma supports growing parts, while sclerenchyma supports mature parts.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

43. Explain the classification of fibers.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Fibres are a type of sclerenchyma that can be classified into different types based on their location, such as xylem fibres, phloem fibres, and cortical fibres.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

44. Describe the structure of vessel elements.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Vessel elements are the main water-conducting cells in the xylem of angiosperms. They are shorter and wider than tracheids and are connected end to end to form a continuous tube.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

45. Explain the structure of tracheids.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Tracheids are elongated, tapering cells in the xylem that transport water and provide support. They are the main water-conducting cells in gymnosperms and ferns.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

46. Describe the structure of sieve tube elements.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Sieve tube elements are the main conducting cells in the phloem. They are arranged end to end to form a sieve tube and have sieve plates at their ends.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

47. Explain the companion cell-sieve tube relationship.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Companion cells are closely associated with sieve tube elements and are connected to them by plasmodesmata. They play a role in the loading and unloading of sugars into the sieve tube.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

48. Describe the loading and unloading of phloem.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Phloem loading is the process of moving sugars from the source (leaves) into the sieve tube, while phloem unloading is the process of moving sugars from the sieve tube to the sink (storage organs or growing parts).

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

49. Explain the cohesion-tension theory related to xylem structure.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The cohesion-tension theory explains the upward movement of water in the xylem. The structure of the xylem, with its continuous column of water, is essential for this process.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

50. Describe the pressure flow hypothesis in relation to phloem anatomy.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The pressure flow hypothesis explains the movement of sugars in the phloem. The anatomy of the phloem, with its sieve tubes and companion cells, is adapted for this process.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Xylem elements differentiate from the procambium. The first-formed xylem is the protoxylem, and the later-formed xylem is the metaxylem.

## SECTION D: LONG ANSWER QUESTIONS (3 marks each) - 100 Questions

**Instructions:** Write detailed answers in 5-6 sentences or provide detailed labeled diagrams.

1. Explain the classification of plant tissues with examples and functions.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Plant tissues are broadly classified into meristematic and permanent tissues. Meristematic tissues are actively dividing and are responsible for growth. They are further classified into apical, intercalary, and lateral meristems. Permanent tissues are derived from meristematic tissues and have lost the ability to divide. They are classified into simple tissues (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) and complex tissues (xylem, phloem).

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

2. Describe the structure and functions of meristematic tissues in detail.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Meristematic tissues are composed of actively dividing, undifferentiated cells. Apical meristems are located at the tips of roots and shoots and are responsible for primary growth. Intercalary meristems are found in grasses and are responsible for the growth of internodes. Lateral meristems, such as the vascular cambium and cork cambium, are responsible for secondary growth.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

3. Compare and contrast the three types of simple permanent tissues.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Parenchyma, collenchyma, and sclerenchyma are three types of simple permanent tissues. Parenchyma cells are thin-walled and are involved in storage and photosynthesis. Collenchyma cells have thickened corners and provide mechanical support to growing parts. Sclerenchyma cells have thick, lignified walls and provide mechanical support to mature parts.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

4. Explain the structure, composition, and functions of xylem tissue.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Xylem is a complex tissue that conducts water and minerals from the roots to the rest of the plant. It is composed of four elements: tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres, and xylem parenchyma. Tracheids and vessels are the main water-conducting cells, while fibres provide support and parenchyma stores food.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

5. Describe the structure, composition, and functions of phloem tissue.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Phloem is a complex tissue that transports food materials from the leaves to other parts of the plant. It is composed of four elements: sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, and phloem fibres. Sieve tube elements are the main conducting cells, while companion cells assist in their function.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

6. Compare the anatomical features of dicot and monocot roots in detail.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Dicot and monocot roots differ in several anatomical features. Dicot roots have a tap root system, fewer xylem bundles (2-4), and a small pith. Monocot roots have a fibrous root system, more xylem bundles (polyarch), and a large pith. Both have a similar arrangement of tissues, including an epidermis, cortex, endodermis, and stele.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

7. Explain the internal structure of dicot root with well-labeled diagram.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

A dicot root has an epidermis with root hairs, a cortex of parenchyma, an endodermis with Casparian strips, and a stele. The stele consists of a pericycle, radial vascular bundles (2-4 xylem and phloem patches), and a small pith. The xylem is exarch.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

8. Describe the anatomy of monocot root and compare it with dicot root.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

A monocot root has a similar anatomy to a dicot root, but it has more than six xylem bundles (polyarch condition) and a large, well-developed pith. It does not undergo secondary growth.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

9. Explain the internal structure of dicot stem with detailed description.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

A dicot stem has an epidermis, a cortex divided into a collenchymatous hypodermis, parenchymatous cortical layers, and an endodermis. The stele has vascular bundles arranged in a ring, which are conjoint, collateral, and open. There is a large pith in the center.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

10. Describe the anatomy of monocot stem and its distinguishing features.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

A monocot stem has a sclerenchymatous hypodermis, scattered vascular bundles, and a large parenchymatous ground tissue. The vascular bundles are conjoint, collateral, and closed. The pith is not distinct.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

11. Compare the anatomical features of dicot and monocot stems.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Dicot and monocot stems differ in the arrangement of their vascular bundles. Dicot stems have vascular bundles in a ring and are open, allowing for secondary growth. Monocot stems have scattered vascular bundles and are closed, so they do not undergo secondary growth.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

12. Explain the structure of dicot leaf and its photosynthetic adaptations.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

A dicot leaf is dorsiventral and has an upper and lower epidermis. The mesophyll is differentiated into an upper palisade parenchyma, which is the main photosynthetic tissue, and a lower spongy parenchyma with air spaces for gas exchange.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

13. Describe the anatomy of monocot leaf and its special features.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

A monocot leaf is isobilateral and has stomata on both surfaces. The mesophyll is not differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma. It may have bulliform cells that help in the rolling of the leaf.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

14. Compare the leaf anatomy of dicots and monocots in detail.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Dicot and monocot leaves differ in their symmetry, stomatal distribution, and mesophyll differentiation. Dicot leaves are dorsiventral with more stomata on the lower surface and a differentiated mesophyll. Monocot leaves are isobilateral with stomata on both surfaces and an undifferentiated mesophyll.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

15. Explain the process and significance of secondary growth in dicot stem.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Secondary growth in a dicot stem is the increase in girth due to the activity of the vascular cambium. The cambium produces secondary xylem to the inside and secondary phloem to the outside. This process is significant for providing support and increasing the conductive capacity of the stem.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

16. Describe the formation of annual rings and their significance.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Annual rings are formed due to the seasonal activity of the vascular cambium. The springwood, with larger vessels, and the autumnwood, with smaller vessels, together form an annual ring. The number of annual rings can be used to determine the age of a tree.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

17. Explain the structure and function of different types of vascular bundles.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Vascular bundles can be radial (in roots), with xylem and phloem on different radii, or conjoint (in stems), with xylem and phloem on the same radius. Conjoint bundles can be collateral (phloem on one side of xylem) or bicollateral (phloem on both sides of xylem).

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

18. Describe the tissue systems in plants and their components.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The tissue systems in plants are the epidermal, ground, and vascular systems. The epidermal system forms the outer protective layer. The ground system fills the space between the epidermis and the vascular system. The vascular system is responsible for transport.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

19. Explain the adaptations in plant anatomy for xerophytic conditions.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Xerophytic plants have anatomical adaptations to conserve water, such as a thick cuticle, sunken stomata, succulent leaves or stems, and a well-developed vascular system.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

20. Describe the anatomical modifications in hydrophytic plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Hydrophytic plants have anatomical modifications to live in water, such as aerenchyma for buoyancy, reduced vascular tissue, and a thin cuticle.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

21. Explain the concept of C4 anatomy and its significance.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

C4 anatomy, or Kranz anatomy, is a specialized leaf anatomy found in C4 plants. It is characterized by a ring of bundle sheath cells around the vascular bundles, which is the site of the Calvin cycle. This anatomy is an adaptation to reduce photorespiration.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

22. Describe the bundle sheath cells and their role in C4 photosynthesis.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The bundle sheath cells in C4 plants are large, have thick walls, and are rich in chloroplasts. They are the site of the Calvin cycle, where carbon dioxide is fixed into sugars.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

23. Explain the formation and structure of bark in woody plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Bark is formed by the activity of the cork cambium, which produces cork to the outside and phelloderm to the inside. Bark includes all the tissues outside the vascular cambium and provides protection to the stem.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

24. Describe the structure and function of different types of secretory tissues.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Secretory tissues in plants include laticiferous ducts (producing latex), resin ducts, nectaries, and hydathodes. These tissues produce and secrete various substances that have different functions in the plant.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

25. Explain the role of mechanical tissues in plant support.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Mechanical tissues, such as collenchyma and sclerenchyma, provide support to the plant body. Collenchyma supports growing parts, while sclerenchyma, with its lignified walls, supports mature parts.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

26. Describe the ontogeny and differentiation of xylem elements.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Xylem elements differentiate from the procambium. The first-formed xylem is the protoxylem, which has smaller vessels, and the later-formed xylem is the metaxylem, which has larger vessels.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

27. Explain the development and maturation of phloem elements.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Phloem elements also differentiate from the procambium. The first-formed phloem is the protophloem, and the later-formed phloem is the metaphloem. The sieve tube elements lose their nucleus at maturity.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

28. Describe the structure and function of cambium in secondary growth.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The cambium is a lateral meristem that is responsible for secondary growth. It is a single layer of cells that divides to produce secondary xylem to the inside and secondary phloem to the outside.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

29. Explain the formation and types of periderm.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Periderm is the outer protective tissue that replaces the epidermis in woody plants. It is formed by the cork cambium and consists of the cork (phellem), cork cambium (phellogen), and phelloderm (secondary cortex).

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

30. Describe the anatomical basis of water transport in plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Water transport in plants occurs through the xylem. The cohesion-tension theory explains the upward movement of water, which is driven by transpiration from the leaves. The anatomical structure of the xylem, with its continuous column of water, is essential for this process.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

31. Explain the anatomical features related to food transport in plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Food transport in plants occurs through the phloem. The pressure flow hypothesis explains the movement of sugars from the source (leaves) to the sink (storage organs or growing parts). The anatomy of the phloem, with its sieve tubes and companion cells, is adapted for this process.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

32. Describe the structure and function of stomatal apparatus.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The stomatal apparatus consists of the stoma (pore), the two guard cells that surround it, and the subsidiary cells. The opening and closing of the stoma are regulated by changes in the turgor pressure of the guard cells.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

33. Explain the anatomical adaptations for gas exchange in plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Gas exchange in plants occurs through the stomata in the leaves and lenticels in the stems. The spongy mesophyll in the leaves has large air spaces that facilitate the diffusion of gases.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

34. Describe the role of endodermis in selective absorption.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The endodermis in the root regulates the selective absorption of water and minerals from the soil into the vascular cylinder. The Casparian strips in the endodermis prevent the apoplastic movement of water.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

35. Explain the structure and significance of Casparian strips.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Casparian strips are bands of suberin in the cell walls of the endodermis that are impermeable to water. They force water to move through the symplast, allowing the plant to control the uptake of water and minerals.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

36. Describe the initiation and development of lateral roots.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Lateral roots are initiated from the pericycle of the parent root. The pericycle cells divide to form a root primordium, which then grows through the cortex and epidermis to emerge as a lateral root.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

37. Explain the anatomical features of storage organs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Storage organs, such as roots, stems, and leaves, have anatomical features adapted for storage. They are typically rich in parenchyma cells that store food in the form of starch, sugars, or oils.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

38. Describe the structure of climbing organs and their adaptations.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Climbing organs, such as tendrils, have anatomical adaptations for climbing. They are sensitive to touch and can coil around a support. Their anatomy is characterized by a well-developed vascular system and mechanical tissues.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

39. Explain the anatomy of protective structures in plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Protective structures in plants, such as thorns and spines, have anatomical adaptations for protection. They are typically hard and pointed and have a large amount of sclerenchyma tissue.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

40. Describe the structure and function of secretory ducts.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Secretory ducts are specialized structures that produce and secrete various substances, such as resin, gum, or oil. They are often found in the cortex or vascular tissues.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

41. Explain the formation and significance of tyloses.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Tyloses are outgrowths of parenchyma cells that block the vessels of the xylem. They are often formed in response to injury or infection and can help to prevent the spread of pathogens.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

42. Describe the anatomical features of reaction wood.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Reaction wood is a type of wood that is formed in response to mechanical stress. It can be tension wood (in angiosperms) or compression wood (in gymnosperms) and has anatomical features that help to support the plant.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

43. Explain the structure and function of transfer cells.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Transfer cells are specialized cells with invaginated cell walls that increase the surface area for transport. They are found in various parts of the plant where there is a high rate of transport, such as in the phloem and nectaries.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

44. Describe the anatomy of mycorrhizal roots.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Mycorrhizal roots have a symbiotic association with fungi. The anatomy of the root is modified to facilitate this association, with the fungal hyphae growing into the root cortex.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

45. Explain the structure of root nodules and their significance.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Root nodules are swellings on the roots of leguminous plants that contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria. The anatomy of the nodule is adapted for this symbiotic relationship, with a central infected zone containing the bacteria.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

46. Describe the anatomical modifications in carnivorous plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Carnivorous plants have anatomical modifications to trap and digest insects. These can include pitcher-shaped leaves, sticky tentacles, or snap traps.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

47. Explain the structure of nectaries and their function.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Nectaries are glands that secrete nectar to attract pollinators. They are often located in the flowers and have a specialized anatomy for nectar secretion.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

48. Describe the anatomy of oil-secreting structures.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Oil-secreting structures, such as glands or ducts, produce and secrete essential oils. They are found in various parts of the plant and have a specialized anatomy for oil secretion.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

49. Explain the formation and structure of resin ducts.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Resin ducts are specialized structures that produce and secrete resin. They are common in gymnosperms and have a specialized anatomy for resin secretion.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

50. Describe the anatomical features of latex-producing plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Latex-producing plants have specialized tubes called laticiferous ducts that produce a milky fluid called latex. These ducts can be articulated or non-articulated.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

51. Explain the structure and function of hydathodes.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Hydathodes are structures that discharge water from the interior of the leaf to its surface, a process called guttation. They are often found at the tips or margins of leaves.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

52. Describe the anatomical adaptations in halophytic plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Halophytic plants have anatomical adaptations to tolerate high salt concentrations, such as succulent leaves, salt glands, and a well-developed vascular system.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

53. Explain the structure of aerenchyma in aquatic plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Aerenchyma is a type of parenchyma with large air spaces that provides buoyancy to aquatic plants and allows for the diffusion of gases.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

54. Describe the anatomical features of epiphytic plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Epiphytic plants have anatomical adaptations to grow on other plants, such as aerial roots for absorption of moisture from the air and specialized leaves for water storage.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

55. Explain the structure and function of pneumatophores.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Pneumatophores are specialized roots that grow upwards into the air to obtain oxygen. Their anatomy is characterized by aerenchyma and lenticels.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

56. Describe the anatomy of contractile roots.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Contractile roots are specialized roots that contract and pull the plant deeper into the soil. Their anatomy is adapted for this function, with a wrinkled surface and a well-developed cortex.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

57. Explain the structure of buttress roots and their function.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Buttress roots are large, woody roots that provide support to tall trees. Their anatomy is similar to that of a stem, with a large amount of secondary xylem.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

58. Describe the anatomical features of parasitic plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Parasitic plants have anatomical adaptations to obtain nutrients from a host plant. They have specialized structures called haustoria that penetrate the host tissue.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

59. Explain the structure of haustoria in parasitic plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Haustoria are specialized organs of parasitic plants that penetrate the host tissue and absorb water and nutrients. Their anatomy is adapted for this function, with a well-developed vascular system.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

60. Describe the anatomy of insectivorous plant traps.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Insectivorous plant traps have a specialized anatomy for trapping and digesting insects. This can include pitcher-shaped leaves, sticky tentacles, or snap traps.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

61. Explain the structure and function of bulliform cells in detail.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Bulliform cells are large, empty, colorless cells found in the epidermis of grasses. They are turgor-operated and help in the rolling and unrolling of leaves in response to water availability.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

62. Describe the anatomical basis of leaf folding mechanisms.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Leaf folding mechanisms are often based on the turgor changes in specialized cells, such as bulliform cells or pulvini. The anatomy of these structures is adapted for this function.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

63. Explain the structure of abscission layers.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Abscission layers are layers of cells at the base of a leaf or fruit that are responsible for its shedding. The cells in this layer undergo enzymatic degradation, leading to the separation of the organ.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

64. Describe the anatomical features of deciduous plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Deciduous plants have anatomical adaptations for shedding their leaves in the autumn, such as the formation of an abscission layer and a protective layer of cork.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

65. Explain the structure and function of lenticels in detail.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Lenticels are pores in the periderm of woody stems that allow for the exchange of gases between the internal tissues and the atmosphere. They are formed by the activity of the cork cambium.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

66. Describe the anatomical adaptations in desert plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Desert plants have anatomical adaptations to conserve water, such as a thick cuticle, sunken stomata, succulent leaves or stems, and a well-developed root system.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

67. Explain the structure of succulent plant anatomy.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Succulent plant anatomy is characterized by the presence of large, water-storing parenchyma cells in the leaves or stems.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

68. Describe the anatomical features of alpine plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Alpine plants have anatomical adaptations to survive in cold, windy, and high-altitude environments, such as a low-growing habit, hairy leaves, and a well-developed root system.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

69. Explain the structure of aquatic plant stems.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Aquatic plant stems have anatomical adaptations to live in water, such as aerenchyma for buoyancy, reduced vascular tissue, and a thin cuticle.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

70. Describe the anatomy of floating leaves.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Floating leaves have anatomical adaptations to float on the surface of the water, such as aerenchyma for buoyancy and stomata on the upper surface.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

71. Explain the structure and function of air chambers in plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Air chambers are large air spaces in the tissues of aquatic plants that provide buoyancy and allow for the diffusion of gases.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

72. Describe the anatomical features of climbing stems.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Climbing stems have anatomical adaptations for climbing, such as tendrils, hooks, or adventitious roots.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

73. Explain the structure of tendrils and their modifications.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Tendrils are modified leaves or stems that are used for climbing. Their anatomy is adapted for coiling and attachment.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

74. Describe the anatomy of thorns and spines.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Thorns and spines are modified stems or leaves that are sharp and pointed, providing protection. Their anatomy is characterized by a large amount of sclerenchyma.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

75. Explain the structure of underground stems.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Underground stems, such as rhizomes, tubers, and corms, have anatomical adaptations for storage and vegetative propagation.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

76. Describe the anatomy of bulbs and their modifications.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Bulbs are modified underground stems with fleshy leaves that store food. Their anatomy is characterized by a reduced stem and large storage leaves.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

77. Explain the structure of tubers and their storage function.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Tubers are swollen underground stems that are used for storage. Their anatomy is characterized by a large amount of storage parenchyma and buds (eyes).

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

78. Describe the anatomy of rhizomes and their characteristics.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Rhizomes are horizontal underground stems that are used for storage and vegetative propagation. Their anatomy is similar to that of a stem, with nodes, internodes, and buds.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

79. Explain the structure of corms and their features.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Corms are condensed, solid underground stems that are used for storage. Their anatomy is similar to that of a stem, with a large amount of storage parenchyma.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

80. Describe the anatomical differences between roots and stems.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Roots and stems differ in their anatomical features. Roots have a root cap, radial vascular bundles, and exarch xylem. Stems have conjoint vascular bundles and endarch xylem.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

81. Explain the structure of transition region between root and stem.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The transition region between the root and the stem is where the anatomical features of the root transition to those of the stem. The vascular bundles change from a radial to a conjoint arrangement.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

82. Describe the anatomical features of monocot flowers.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Monocot flowers have floral parts in multiples of three. Their anatomy is similar to that of other flowers, with sepals, petals, stamens, and pistils.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

83. Explain the structure of dicot flowers.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Dicot flowers have floral parts in multiples of four or five. Their anatomy is similar to that of other flowers, with sepals, petals, stamens, and pistils.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

84. Describe the anatomy of fruits and their development.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Fruits develop from the ovary of a flower after fertilization. Their anatomy is related to their function in protecting and dispersing the seeds.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

85. Explain the structure of seeds and their anatomical features.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Seeds develop from the ovules of a flower after fertilization. Their anatomy includes a seed coat, an embryo, and a food storage tissue (endosperm or cotyledons).

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

86. Describe the anatomical changes during seed germination.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

During seed germination, the embryo grows and develops into a seedling. The anatomical changes include the emergence of the radicle and the plumule.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

87. Explain the structure of seedlings and their development.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Seedlings are young plants that have recently germinated from a seed. Their anatomy includes a primary root, a primary shoot, and cotyledons.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

88. Describe the anatomical features of annual plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Annual plants complete their life cycle in one year. Their anatomy is adapted for rapid growth and reproduction.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

89. Explain the structure of perennial plant organs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Perennial plants live for more than two years. Their anatomy is adapted for survival over multiple seasons, often with storage organs and secondary growth.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

90. Describe the anatomical adaptations in biennial plants.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Biennial plants complete their life cycle in two years. Their anatomy is adapted for vegetative growth in the first year and reproduction in the second year.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

91. Explain the structure of compound leaves.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Compound leaves have a lamina that is divided into multiple leaflets. Their anatomy is similar to that of simple leaves, but with a rachis connecting the leaflets.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

92. Describe the anatomy of simple leaves.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Simple leaves have a single, undivided lamina. Their anatomy includes an epidermis, mesophyll, and vascular bundles.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

93. Explain the structure of leaf sheaths.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Leaf sheaths are the basal part of a leaf that encloses the stem. Their anatomy is adapted for providing support and protection.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

94. Describe the anatomy of leaf stipules.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Leaf stipules are small, leaf-like appendages at the base of a leaf. Their anatomy is similar to that of a small leaf.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

95. Explain the structure of modified leaves.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Modified leaves, such as tendrils, spines, and storage leaves, have anatomical adaptations for their specific functions.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

96. Describe the anatomical features of bracts.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Bracts are modified leaves that are associated with a flower or inflorescence. Their anatomy is often simpler than that of a foliage leaf.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

97. Explain the structure of sepals and petals.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Sepals and petals are the outer whorls of a flower. Their anatomy is similar to that of a leaf, but they are often specialized for protection or attraction.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

98. Describe the anatomy of stamens and pistils.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Stamens and pistils are the reproductive parts of a flower. Their anatomy is adapted for the production of pollen and ovules.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

99. Explain the structure of ovules and their development.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

Ovules are the structures within the ovary that develop into seeds after fertilization. Their anatomy includes an integument, a nucellus, and an embryo sac.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

100. Describe the anatomical basis of fruit and seed dispersal mechanisms.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

The anatomical features of fruits and seeds are often related to their dispersal mechanisms, such as wings for wind dispersal, fleshy tissues for animal dispersal, or hooks for attachment to fur.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

## Section C: Short Answer Questions (2 marks each) - 100 Questions

1. Describe the body divisions and absent structures in a frog.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Body Divisions:** The frog's body is divided into a head and a trunk. A distinct neck and a tail are absent, which gives the frog its characteristic stout appearance.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

2. Explain the characteristics of frog skin and its coloration.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Skin Characteristics:** The skin is moist, smooth, and slippery due to mucus secretion, which aids in cutaneous respiration. The dorsal side is olive green with dark spots for camouflage, while the ventral side is pale yellow.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

3. Describe the structure and function of frog eyes.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Eyes:** The eyes are large and bulging, providing a wide field of view. They are protected by a nictitating membrane, which is a transparent third eyelid that allows the frog to see underwater and keeps the eyes moist on land.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

4. Explain the limb structure and digit arrangement in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Limbs:** Frogs have two pairs of limbs. The forelimbs are short with four digits and are used for propping the body up. The hind limbs are large and muscular with five webbed digits, adapted for powerful leaping and swimming.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

5. Describe the sexual dimorphism observed in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Sexual Dimorphism:** Male frogs are distinguished from females by the presence of sound-producing vocal sacs, which are used to make mating calls. They also have a copulatory pad on the first digit of their forelimbs to help grasp the female during mating.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

6. Explain why the alimentary canal of a frog is short and what this indicates about their feeding habits.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Alimentary Canal:** The alimentary canal is short because frogs are carnivores, and meat is easier and faster to digest than plant material (cellulose). This indicates a diet of insects and other small animals.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

7. Trace the path of food from mouth to cloaca in a frog.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Path of Food:** Food enters the mouth, goes to the buccal cavity, then through the pharynx and oesophagus into the stomach. From the stomach, it moves to the intestine, then the rectum, and undigested waste is expelled through the cloaca.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

8. Describe the digestive glands and their functions in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Digestive Glands:** The liver secretes bile, which is stored in the gall bladder and helps in fat digestion. The pancreas produces pancreatic juice containing various enzymes that break down carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

9. Explain the process of food capture and digestion in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Food Capture and Digestion:** A frog captures its prey using its sticky, bilobed tongue. Digestion begins in the stomach with gastric juices and is completed in the intestine by enzymes from the pancreas and intestinal wall.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

10. Describe the different types of respiration in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Respiration:** Frogs have three modes of respiration. In water, they use cutaneous respiration (skin). On land, they use buccal respiration (mouth lining) and pulmonary respiration (lungs).

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

11. Explain the structure and location of frog lungs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Lungs:** The lungs are a pair of elongated, pink-colored, sac-like structures located in the upper part of the trunk (thorax). They are less efficient than mammalian lungs and are supplemented by other respiratory surfaces.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

12. Describe the respiratory process on land in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Respiration on Land:** Air is drawn into the buccal cavity through the nostrils. The frog then closes its nostrils and mouth, and raises the floor of the buccal cavity, forcing air into the lungs.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

13. Explain the structure of the frog's heart and its chambers.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Heart Structure:** The frog has a three-chambered heart, consisting of two upper chambers called atria (right and left) and a single lower chamber called the ventricle. This structure leads to some mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

14. Describe the components of frog blood and their characteristics.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Blood Components:** Frog blood consists of plasma (the liquid matrix) and blood cells. The cells include erythrocytes (RBCs), which are oval, biconvex, and nucleated, leucocytes (WBCs), and platelets.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

15. Explain the blood circulation pattern in a frog's heart.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Blood Circulation:** Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium, while oxygenated blood from the lungs and skin enters the left atrium. Both empty into the single ventricle, where the blood gets mixed before being pumped out to the body.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

16. Describe the lymphatic system in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Lymphatic System:** This system is separate from the blood circulatory system and consists of lymph (a fluid similar to blood but lacking RBCs), lymph channels, and lymph nodes. It is involved in fluid balance and immunity.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

17. Explain the structure and location of frog kidneys.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Kidneys:** Frogs have a pair of compact, dark red, bean-like kidneys. They are located in the posterior part of the body cavity, on either side of the vertebral column.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

18. Describe the excretory pathway in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Excretory Pathway:** Nitrogenous waste (urea) is filtered from the blood by the kidneys to form urine. The urine travels down the ureters to the cloaca, from where it can be stored in the urinary bladder or expelled.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

19. Explain the difference between excretory systems in male and female frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Male vs. Female Excretory System:** In males, the ureters also carry sperm and are thus called urinogenital ducts. In females, the ureters and the oviducts are separate and open independently into the cloaca.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

20. Describe the organization of the nervous system in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Nervous System Organization:** The nervous system is organized into the Central Nervous System (CNS), which includes the brain and spinal cord, and the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS), which consists of cranial and spinal nerves. There is also an Autonomic Nervous System (ANS).

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

21. Explain the structure and divisions of the frog brain.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Brain Divisions:** The brain is divided into three main parts: the fore-brain (responsible for smell and thought), the mid-brain (responsible for vision), and the hind-brain (responsible for balance and involuntary actions).

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

22. Describe the forebrain and its components.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Forebrain:** The forebrain consists of the olfactory lobes (for sense of smell), paired cerebral hemispheres (the main thinking part), and an unpaired diencephalon.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

23. Explain the structure and function of the midbrain.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Midbrain:** The midbrain is characterized by a pair of optic lobes, which are the primary centers for the sense of sight in the frog.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

24. Describe the hindbrain and its components.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Hindbrain:** The hindbrain is composed of the cerebellum, which controls balance and coordination, and the medulla oblongata, which controls involuntary functions like heartbeat and respiration.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

25. Explain the male reproductive system in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Male Reproductive System:** This consists of a pair of yellowish, ovoid testes attached to the kidneys by a fold called the mesorchium. Sperm travels from the testes through the vasa efferentia to the kidneys.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

26. Describe the pathway of sperm from testes to cloaca.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Sperm Pathway:** Sperm from the testes pass through the vasa efferentia into the Bidder's canal in the kidney. From there, they travel through the urinogenital duct (the ureter) and are released through the cloaca.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

27. Explain the female reproductive system in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Female Reproductive System:** This consists of a pair of large, lobulated ovaries located near the kidneys. A pair of coiled oviducts arises from the ovaries and opens separately into the cloaca.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

28. Describe the reproductive capacity of female frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Female Reproductive Capacity:** A mature female frog is capable of laying a large number of eggs at once, typically between 2,500 and 3,000 ova, to increase the chances of survival in an external fertilization scenario.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

29. Explain the process of fertilization in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Fertilization:** Fertilization is external and occurs in water. The male frog clasps the female (amplexus) and releases sperm over the eggs as the female lays them.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

30. Describe the development pattern in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Development:** The development is indirect, meaning it includes a larval stage. The fertilized egg develops into a tadpole, which is aquatic and very different from the adult frog. The tadpole then undergoes metamorphosis to become an adult.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

31. Explain the adaptations of frog skin for respiration.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Skin Respiration Adaptations:** The frog's skin is thin, highly vascularized (rich in blood vessels), and kept moist by mucus glands. This allows dissolved oxygen to diffuse directly from the air or water into the blood.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

32. Describe the adaptations of hind limbs for aquatic life.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Hind Limb Aquatic Adaptations:** The hind limbs are long and muscular for powerful strokes. The digits are connected by a web of skin, which increases the surface area to push against the water, making swimming more efficient.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

33. Explain the mechanism of food capture in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Food Capture Mechanism:** The frog's tongue is attached at the front of the mouth, not the back. It can be rapidly flicked out and its sticky, bilobed tip adheres to prey like insects, which are then drawn back into the mouth.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

34. Describe the role of bile in frog digestion.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Role of Bile:** Bile, produced by the liver, is an emulsifying agent. It breaks down large fat globules in the food into smaller droplets, increasing the surface area for fat-digesting enzymes (lipases) to act upon.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

35. Explain the concept of cutaneous respiration.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Cutaneous Respiration:** This is the process of gas exchange (breathing) that occurs across the skin rather than through lungs or gills. It is a major mode of respiration for frogs, especially when they are in water or hibernating.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

36. Describe the advantages of having a three-chambered heart.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Advantages of Three-Chambered Heart:** While it allows some mixing of blood, it is more advanced than a two-chambered heart. It partially separates the pulmonary (to the lungs) and systemic (to the body) circuits, allowing for higher blood pressure than in fish.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

37. Explain the disadvantages of incomplete double circulation.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Disadvantages of Incomplete Double Circulation:** The mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in the single ventricle means the blood delivered to the body is not fully oxygenated. This limits the frog's maximum metabolic rate and sustained activity level.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

38. Describe the excretory adaptations in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Excretory Adaptations:** Frogs excrete urea, which is less toxic than ammonia and requires less water to flush out, a useful adaptation for time spent on land. The kidneys are efficient at filtering waste while conserving water when necessary.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

39. Explain the nervous control mechanisms in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Nervous Control:** The frog's well-developed brain and nervous system allow for complex behaviors like hunting, escaping predators, and mating. The hindbrain controls vital functions, while the forebrain allows for basic learning and instinctual behaviors.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

40. Describe the hormonal control of reproduction in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Hormonal Control of Reproduction:** Reproduction is controlled by hormones from the pituitary gland and gonads. These hormones trigger the development of gametes (sperm and eggs) and secondary sexual characteristics during the breeding season.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

41. Explain the significance of external fertilization.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Significance of External Fertilization:** This strategy requires water, tying the frog's reproduction to an aquatic environment. Laying a large number of eggs compensates for the high mortality rate of eggs and tadpoles due to predation and environmental hazards.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

42. Describe the advantages of indirect development.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Advantages of Indirect Development:** The larval (tadpole) and adult stages occupy different ecological niches. The tadpole is typically an aquatic herbivore, while the adult is a terrestrial carnivore, which prevents competition for food and resources between the young and adults.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

43. Explain the process of metamorphosis in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Metamorphosis Process:** This is a hormonally controlled (by thyroxine) process where the tadpole undergoes drastic changes. It loses its gills and tail, develops lungs and limbs, and its digestive system changes to adapt from a herbivorous to a carnivorous diet.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

44. Describe the structural adaptations for amphibious life.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Amphibious Adaptations:** Frogs show adaptations for both water and land. These include moist, permeable skin for respiration in both environments, powerful webbed hind limbs for swimming and jumping, and lungs for breathing on land.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

45. Explain the respiratory adaptations for dual habitat.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Respiratory Adaptations for Dual Habitat:** Frogs can switch between cutaneous respiration (predominant in water) and pulmonary/buccal respiration (used on land). This versatility allows them to exploit both aquatic and terrestrial environments effectively.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

46. Describe the circulatory adaptations in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Circulatory Adaptations:** The three-chambered heart and double circulation (though incomplete) allow for more efficient blood flow than in fish. The circulatory system is adapted to supply oxygen from both the lungs and the skin to the body tissues.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

47. Explain the excretory adaptations for aquatic environment.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Excretory Adaptations for Aquatic Environment:** When in water, frogs can produce large amounts of dilute urine to get rid of excess water that enters the body by osmosis. On land, they conserve water by producing more concentrated urine.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

48. Describe the nervous system adaptations for survival.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Nervous System Survival Adaptations:** The frog's nervous system is adapted for quick reflexes, essential for catching fast-moving insects and escaping predators. The large optic lobes indicate a heavy reliance on vision for hunting and survival.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

49. Explain the reproductive adaptations for aquatic breeding.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Reproductive Adaptations for Aquatic Breeding:** Frogs return to water to breed, where external fertilization is possible. The eggs are laid in water, and the larval tadpole stage is fully aquatic, completing its development in the water before moving to land.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

50. Describe the morphological adaptations for jumping.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Morphological Adaptations for Jumping:** Frogs have long, muscular hind limbs and a rigid pelvic girdle that is fused to the vertebral column. This provides a strong, stable base for the powerful thrust generated by the leg muscles during a jump.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

51. Explain the digestive adaptations for carnivorous diet.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Digestive Adaptations for Carnivorous Diet:** The short alimentary canal is typical for carnivores as protein is digested relatively quickly. The wide mouth and protrusible tongue are adaptations for capturing and swallowing live prey whole.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

52. Describe the sensory adaptations in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Sensory Adaptations:** Frogs have well-developed eyes for vision, a tympanum for hearing, and chemoreceptors on the skin and in the mouth for taste and smell. These senses are crucial for finding food, avoiding predators, and locating mates.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

53. Explain the protective adaptations of frog skin.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Protective Adaptations of Skin:** The skin's coloration provides camouflage against predators. Glandular secretions can make the frog slippery and hard to grasp, and some species have poison glands that secrete toxins as a defense mechanism.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

54. Describe the locomotory adaptations in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Locomotory Adaptations:** Frogs are adapted for two primary modes of locomotion. They use their powerful hind limbs for jumping on land (saltatorial locomotion) and for swimming in water, aided by their webbed feet.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

55. Explain the feeding adaptations in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Feeding Adaptations:** The primary feeding adaptation is the protractible, sticky tongue used to catch insects. Frogs are opportunistic predators and will attempt to eat almost any animal they can swallow.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

56. Describe the breathing adaptations for dual life.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Breathing Adaptations for Dual Life:** The ability to use skin, lungs, and the lining of the mouth for gas exchange provides great flexibility. This allows the frog to remain submerged for long periods or to be active on land.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

57. Explain the circulatory system efficiency in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Circulatory System Efficiency:** While the mixing of blood in the ventricle makes it less efficient than a four-chambered heart, the system is efficient enough to support the frog's ectothermic ("cold-blooded") metabolism and bursts of activity.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

58. Describe the excretory system efficiency in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Excretory System Efficiency:** The kidneys are efficient at filtering waste from the blood. The ability to produce either dilute or concentrated urine allows the frog to maintain water balance (osmoregulation) in different environments.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

59. Explain the nervous system organization in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Nervous System Organization:** The frog's nervous system is more centralized than in invertebrates, with a distinct brain and spinal cord. This allows for coordinated movements and more complex behaviors.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

60. Describe the reproductive system efficiency in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Reproductive System Efficiency:** Frogs produce a very large number of eggs to counteract the low survival rate associated with external fertilization and lack of parental care. This "numbers game" strategy is effective for species survival.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

61. Explain the importance of moist skin in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Importance of Moist Skin:** Moist skin is essential for cutaneous respiration, as gases can only diffuse across a moist surface. The mucus also provides protection against pathogens and makes the frog slippery to predators.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

62. Describe the role of webbed feet in frog locomotion.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Role of Webbed Feet:** The webbing between the digits of the hind limbs increases the surface area of the foot. This allows the frog to push more effectively against the water, making it a powerful and efficient swimmer.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

63. Explain the significance of bilobed tongue in feeding.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Significance of Bilobed Tongue:** The forked, or bilobed, shape of the tongue, combined with its sticky surface, increases the area available to trap an insect. It is flicked out rapidly to ensnare prey.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

64. Describe the role of vocal sacs in frog reproduction.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Role of Vocal Sacs:** Vocal sacs are pouches of skin in male frogs that inflate and act as resonating chambers. They amplify the mating calls, allowing them to be heard over long distances to attract females.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

65. Explain the function of copulatory pads in male frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Function of Copulatory Pads:** These are rough pads on the first digit of a male frog's forelimbs. They provide a strong grip on the female's slippery skin during amplexus (mating embrace), ensuring the male is in the correct position to fertilize the eggs as they are laid.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

66. Describe the role of nictitating membrane in eye protection.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Role of Nictitating Membrane:** This is a transparent third eyelid that can be drawn over the eye. It protects the eye from debris and predators underwater while still allowing the frog to see, and it keeps the eye moist on land.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

67. Explain the function of tympanum in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Function of Tympanum:** The tympanum is the eardrum, a circular membrane located behind the eye. It vibrates in response to sound waves and transmits these vibrations to the inner ear, allowing the frog to hear both in air and water.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

68. Describe the digestive enzyme production in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Digestive Enzyme Production:** Digestive enzymes are produced by the stomach lining (e.g., pepsin) and the pancreas (e.g., amylase, lipase, trypsin). These enzymes are crucial for breaking down complex food molecules into smaller, absorbable units.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

69. Explain the absorption mechanism in frog intestine.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Absorption in Intestine:** The inner wall of the intestine has numerous folds called villi and microvilli. These structures vastly increase the surface area available for the absorption of digested nutrients into the bloodstream.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

70. Describe the gas exchange mechanism in frog lungs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Gas Exchange in Lungs:** In the simple, sac-like lungs, air is brought in, and oxygen diffuses across the thin, moist, alveolar surfaces into the rich network of capillaries. Carbon dioxide diffuses in the opposite direction, from the blood into the lungs to be exhaled.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

71. Explain the blood circulation pattern in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Blood Circulation Pattern:** Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium, and oxygenated blood from the lungs/skin enters the left atrium. They mix in the ventricle, which pumps blood to the body (systemic circulation) and back to the lungs/skin (pulmonary circulation).

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

72. Describe the urine formation process in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Urine Formation:** Blood is filtered under pressure in the kidneys. Useful substances like glucose and water are reabsorbed back into the blood, while waste products like urea and excess salts are concentrated into urine.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

73. Explain the nerve impulse transmission in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Nerve Impulse Transmission:** Sensory nerves transmit signals from sense organs to the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord). The CNS processes the information and sends motor signals via motor nerves to muscles and glands to produce a response.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

74. Describe the hormone production in frog reproduction.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Hormone Production in Reproduction:** The pituitary gland in the brain releases hormones that stimulate the testes in males to produce testosterone and the ovaries in females to produce estrogen. These hormones regulate gamete formation and mating behavior.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

75. Explain the egg laying process in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Egg Laying Process:** A mature female frog's ovaries release thousands of eggs into the body cavity. These eggs are then guided into the oviducts, where they are coated with a gelatinous layer before being expelled through the cloaca into the water.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

76. Describe the sperm transport mechanism in male frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Sperm Transport in Males:** Sperm are produced in the testes and travel through fine tubes called vasa efferentia into the kidneys. They then pass through the ureters (which function as urinogenital ducts) and are discharged through the cloaca.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

77. Explain the tadpole adaptations for aquatic life.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Tadpole Aquatic Adaptations:** Tadpoles are well-adapted for life in water. They have gills for breathing, a tail for swimming, and a lateral line system to detect water movements. Their mouthparts are adapted for scraping algae.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

78. Describe the metamorphic changes in frog development.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Metamorphic Changes:** During metamorphosis, the tadpole undergoes a complete transformation. It develops lungs as its gills disappear, limbs grow, the tail is reabsorbed, and the digestive system changes to accommodate a carnivorous diet.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

79. Explain the adult frog adaptations for terrestrial life.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Adult Frog Terrestrial Adaptations:** The adult frog is adapted for land with lungs for breathing, strong limbs for jumping, and skin that can resist some water loss. Its excretory system is also adapted to conserve water when not in an aquatic environment.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

80. Describe the seasonal adaptations in frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Seasonal Adaptations:** Frogs are ectothermic and their activity is dependent on temperature. They undergo hibernation (winter dormancy) in cold climates and estivation (summer dormancy) in hot, dry climates to survive unfavorable conditions.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

81. Explain the feeding behavior of adult frogs.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Feeding Behavior of Adult Frogs:** Adult frogs are typically ambush predators. They sit and wait for prey, such as insects, spiders, or worms, to come within range. They then use their powerful tongue to capture the prey with a rapid flick.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

82. Describe the breathing pattern changes during development.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Breathing Pattern Changes during Development:** The larval tadpole breathes exclusively through gills. During metamorphosis, the gills degenerate and are replaced by lungs. The adult frog uses a combination of lungs, skin, and buccal cavity for respiration.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

83. Explain the circulatory changes during metamorphosis.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">

**Circulatory Changes during Metamorphosis:** The circulatory system is remodeled during metamorphosis. The aortic arches that supplied the gills are modified to form the new arteries that supply the lungs and the rest of the body in the adult frog.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

84. Describe the excretory changes during development.
<Accordions>
  <Accordion title="Show Answer">
